title: Compact change-set indexing playbook
body:
Purpose:
- Sketch a small, stable index format and a set of operational rules for compact change-set records used to accelerate session snapshot discovery and patch application in edge/local LLM proxies.
- This playbook is intentionally conservative: minimal fields, cheap comparisons, tolerant to partial data, and easy to read/repair with standard tooling.

Motivation / constraints:
- We need sub-ms lookups for "hot" session fragments (small deltas) in the proxy without querying the primary catalog.
- Payloads are short (typically < 4KB compressed) but there will be many versions per user (dozens -> hundreds).
- Indexes must fit in memory-friendly structures and survive cold-start with simple rebuilds.
- Backward compatible: we must be tolerant when newer agents write fields older agents ignore.
- Repairability: ops can sed/awk the flat index on the fly. No protobuf-only binary blobs.

High-level idea:
- Keep a line-delimited, compact, stable index file per tenant on local proxy: index.v1.ldjson (ldjson = line-delimited JSON) or CSV-lite.
- Each line = one change-set index entry. Entries are append-only; compacted by periodic background sweep.
- Index used for: existence check, quick candidate ranking, eviction decisions, and prefetch hints.

Minimal index fields (v0):
- change_id: short stable id (base62-ish)
- parent_id: immediate parent snapshot id (optional)
- anchor_hash: small fingerprint of content that helps fast equality checks (32-bit hex)
- token_span: approximate token count (int)
- created_ts: unix epoch seconds
- ttl_s: optional ttl relative to created_ts; 0 means immortal
- size_bytes: compressed payload size (int)
- quality_tag: short tag (e.g. "prefetch", "gold", "ephemeral")
- store_hint: one of [local, remote, cold] (small set for routing)
- checksum: crc32 of the payload (optional but helpful)

One-line example (ldjson):
{"change_id":"c2k9","parent_id":"c2k8","anchor_hash":"a7f3b1","token_span":"186","created_ts":"1730889600","ttl_s":"0","size_bytes":"3320","quality_tag":"prefetch","store_hint":"local","checksum":"9f3d2b8a"}

CSV-lite example (space-delimited, stable order):
change_id parent_id anchor_hash token_span created_ts ttl_s size_bytes quality_tag store_hint checksum
c2k9 c2k8 a7f3b1 186 1730889600 0 3320 prefetch local 9f3d2b8a

Why both?
- ldjson is readable and extensible; CSV-lite is a faster, minimal parser for constrained agents. Accept either but prefer ldjson for new writes.

Index operations:
- write_append(entry): append new line. Writers should use O_APPEND semantics. If local FS doesn't support atomic append, write to tmp+rename.
- read_scan(range_ts): streaming read scanning from newest to oldest up to N lines to find recent candidates.
- lookup_by_change_id(id): in-memory hashmap built at startup; if missing, falls back to scan.
- compact(): rewrite a fresh index file keeping the newest entry per change_id and evicting expired entries. Should be rate-limited and cooperative with runtime.
- repair_tool: simple awk/sed script that extracts syntactically valid lines and reserializes them; keep repair journal.

Memory layout suggestion on proxy start:
- stream index file and build small in-memory shard index: change_id -> (offset, size_bytes, anchor_hash, created_ts, ttl_s). Store only 48 bytes per entry on average.
- limit map to top-K recent entries via LRU if memory low.

Eviction/compaction policy (starter):
1) Drop entries with ttl_s > 0 && created_ts + ttl_s < now.
2) Keep entries with quality_tag=="gold" regardless of size until space pressure.
3) Evict oldest by created_ts when total size_bytes across entries > quota (tenant-configurable).
4) On write overflow, if a new entry has store_hint==local and size_bytes < evictable_average, allow write and schedule async compact.

Routing hints and cheat-sheet for routing decisions:
- store_hint==local => prefer local cache + faster checksum verification; if missing, fall back to remote.
- store_hint==cold => index entry present but payload likely only on remote. Use for low-latency rank filters only.
- quality_tag==prefetch => preemptively rehydrate on warm-up windows (e.g., after first N requests).

Operations playbook (quick):
- Rebuild: cat index.v1.ldjson | jq -c . > index.clean && mv index.clean index.v1.ldjson (keep backup).
- Compaction: run compactor as separate process with pid file. Compactor holds write lock. If compactor dies, leave tombstone file and let next compactor resume.
- Corruption handling: on parse errors, move index.v1.ldjson -> index.v1.corrupt.TIMESTAMP and reconstruct from the last checkpoint (index.checkpoint) + transaction log.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Use numeric token_span vs. more precise byte-range anchors? Numeric is smaller but less precise.
- Should we include model_id or model_variant in index? Pros: faster compatibility checks; Cons: index churn when model updates. Maybe optional field in v1.
- Signatures: do we need signed entries to detect tampering in on-prem proxies? Could add optional signature field.
- Sharding: single file per tenant vs. per-worker files. Per-worker avoids locks but complicates warm lookup.

Next steps (practical):
- Pick final field set for v0 and implement writer/reader library in Go/Python (start with Go).
- Implement compacting job with unit tests for concurrency and crash scenarios.
- Add a small CLI: index-inspect, index-compact, index-repair.
- Prototype read performance on sample tenant with 100k entries, measure cold-start map build time and memory.

Notes to self (TODO):
- Add simple binary encoding option (TLV with fixed tags) for agents that want very compact indexes. Keep compatibility via small header.
- Discuss store_hint semantics with SRE; ensure hints are helpful and not abused.
- Draft migration plan for existing snapshot indices to v0 format (bulk convert script).

Rough ASCII of usage path:
client -> local proxy lookup (in-memory map) -> if hit and store_hint==local then fetch payload -> verify checksum -> apply patch -> respond
                                     
                         miss -> fall back to remote catalog -> fetch -> insert index append -> respond

Small failure scenarios to test:
- concurrent writers on network FS (simulate O_APPEND failures).
- partial line append due to crash. Recovery should skip partial line and resume.
- index grows too large and compactor can't free space because of pinned "gold" entries (operator override).

Endnotes: this is a working sketch. Intend to iterate after perf numbers and early infra runs. Keep it small and auditable.

-- maya
